extracted.intended_audience: legal commentators, political pamphleteers, lawyers and informed public (18th-century style political/legal writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for composing and arguing in political pamphlets and legal commentary, especially on parliamentary law, use of precedent, and how to address the public. Emphasises completeness, fair use of authorities, interpretive care, and audience/medium choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with professed intention
rubrics_metrics.description: A pamphlet written to defend one's reputation should confine itself to that defence rather than mixing sustained attacks on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius: 'It would have been more consistent, perhaps, with your professed intention, to have confined yourself to the last.' Avoid wandering from the declared purpose of a piece; mixing unrelated attacks and defenses undermines coherence and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability and completeness in legal commentaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal work treating the law of parliament should foresee probable cases and state how far parliamentary powers extend in such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius criticises Blackstone for omitting discussion of whether expulsion alone creates disqualification; guidance: when treating the constitution or parliamentary law, anticipate plausible scenarios (e.g., temporary incapacities lasting years) and state limits of authority so affected parties (e.g., electors) can act knowledgeably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim exhaustiveness unless exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer affirms that every case is included, but has omitted a material case, that amounts to laying a snare for the unwary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote and text: 'If, in stating the law upon any point, a judge deliberately affirms that he has included every case, and it should appear that he has purposely omitted a material case, he does, in effect, lay a snare for the unwary.' Practical rule: avoid blanket statements of completeness unless one has in fact covered all material situations; if making enumerations, be explicit about scope and caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity when enumerating disqualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a long enumeration of disqualifications concludes with words implying 'every subject of the realm is eligible of common right', a reader will naturally assume no species of disqualification was omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius points out that authoritative works (like Commentaries) create expectations of completeness; guidance: when listing legal disqualifications, be precise about whether the list is exhaustive and explicitly note any extraordinary or temporary incapacities that might fall outside ordinary categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise general nature of laws despite particular applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are general even if applied in a particular case; an instance affecting an individual reflects a general legal rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius: 'though the instance in which a penal law is exerted be particular, the laws themselves are general.' When explaining law, articulate its general scope and public consequences rather than treating individual cases as isolated anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include extraordinary privileges/rights when treating constitutional topics
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing the constitution of the House of Commons and related laws and customs, one must take notice of extraordinary and arbitrary privileges (e.g., power of expulsion and its consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius criticises omission of the right to expel and its effect on eligibility: 'you certainly were guilty of a most unpardonable omission.' Guidance for writers: do not omit discussion of powers or privileges with large public consequences when treating constitutional subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of precedent: present the whole precedent, not selective parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In fair argument, no part of a precedent should be admitted unless the whole of it be given together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius admonishes opponents who cite only parts of the Walpole precedent: 'In fair argument, no part of a precedent shoud be admitted, unless the whole of it be given to us together.' Guidance: when relying on precedents, reproduce full text/context and consider subsequent votes/related resolutions—cherry-picking segments is disingenuous and may invert meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider changes in law and differing historical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking historical cases, recognise that the law of elections or parliamentary practice may have changed and that earlier precedents might have been decided under different rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius argues that even if Walpole and the Middlesex cases appear similar, they occurred under different legal regimes: 'It will only prove, that the law of election, at that time, was different from the present law.' Writers should compare contexts and avoid treating old resolutions as dispositive without analysing their contemporaneous legal framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret legal votes and resolutions by their explicit wording and stated causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the text of a vote/resolution to infer the cause of a declared legal consequence; if a vote lists crimes and punishment, the incapacity is declared to arise from the crimes, not merely from the expulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the Walpole vote as example, Junius notes the vote specifies 'committed a prisoner to the Tower, and expelled...for a high breach of trust...and notorious corruption' and concludes the incapacity derives from the crimes. Guidance: do not infer legal effects (e.g., incapacity) from procedural acts alone without considering the explicit reasons the authoritative body recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-law principle: null votes are nonentities and do not subtract from others
rubrics_metrics.description: If votes given to an incapable candidate are null and void, they cannot be opposed to the votes given to another candidate; such null votes are mere nonentities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius: 'it is...the known and established law of the land... that if the votes given to one candidate are null and void, they cannot be opposed to the votes given to another candidate.' Guidance: in assessing election results where an ineligible candidate receives votes, treat those votes as having no legal effect rather than as subtractive or otherwise altering qualified candidates' tallies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose channel and tone appropriate to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing to inform the body of the people, prefer channels and styles that will spread farthest rather than lengthy quartos aimed at the learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junius: 'I prefer that channel of conveyance which is likely to spread farthest among them.' Guidance for political writers: select medium (newspaper vs. quarto) and adopt accessible tone when the goal is popular persuasion; do not assume verbosity or size confer authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sophistry and selective argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not descend to 'unworthy artifices' such as treacherous compilation, false quotations, or dividing a precedent to suit one's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple passages criticise opponents for selective quoting and sophistry. Practical rule: present honest citations, avoid misleading recitations, and address the strongest contrary arguments rather than relying on rhetorical tricks.
